topic: C++ Coding Agents: AI Pair Programming for Systems Development

key_points: C++ repos score lowest (median 42/100) on agent-readiness: 88% pin no toolchain version (agent hits template errors unrelated to its edit), 78% commit no dependency pinning, 78% leave no discoverable test command.
No standard package manager means an agent cannot reliably install or verify a project; writing commands down changes the most in C++.
AGENTS.md is the tool-agnostic file that every agent reads; CLAUDE.md/.cursorrules are tool-specific and still work.
Core guidance: write install command (cmake -B build) and verify command (ctest --test-dir build) so an agent can start and self-check.
Memory-safety bugs make up 65-70% of high/critical vulnerabilities in Chrome, Android, iOS, Windows, Linux kernel year after year.
C/C++ are worst-served by static analysis; NSA (2022) recommended switching to memory-safe languages, while Stroustrup argues for making C++ safer instead (RAII, smart pointers, span, enforcement).
AI agents imitate the patterns around them, so in old C++ codebases they reproduce memory-corruption bugs faster than humans can review; agents inherit ecosystem-specific failure modes.
Sanitizers are the closest C/C++ runtime safety net but are opt-in and only flag bugs on tested paths; static alone isn't a control at agent speed.
84% of developers use or plan to use AI tools (Stack Overflow 2025), up from 76% in 2024.
90% of professional developers regularly used an AI coding tool at work by January 2026 (JetBrains AI Pulse).
GitHub Copilot leads world work adoption at 29%; Cursor and Claude Code each at 18%.
AI code-assistant market ~$3.5B (Gartner 2025); GitHub Copilot 20M+ cumulative users, 4.7M paid subscribers (Jan 2026).
Dedicated C++ agent skills exist (e.g. cpp-pro) for modern C++20/23, template metaprogramming, concepts, ranges, coroutines, SIMD, memory management, CMake build config.
The value of a C++-specific prompt/skill is focusing agents on performance, concurrency, and memory-management concerns rather than generic codegen.
CMake skill patterns: out-of-source builds, generator selection (Ninja/Make), target_link_libraries, find_package, FetchContent, sanitizers, toolchain files for cross-compile.
For large refactors, agentic-loop tools (Claude Code) read files as needed and maintain a codebase mental model across tool calls; IDE-composer tools (Cursor) depend on you @-mentioning files.
Context fills fast on large refactors; run tests after each extracted module to avoid partial-refactor regressions.
Hybrid pattern: use Cursor for granular single-file work and a CLI agent for cross-file refactors, verifying with full test suite after each phase.

angles: Why C++ is the hardest (yet highest-value) language for AI coding agents: build-system diversity, templates, memory safety, no standard package manager, and decades of legacy C-style hot paths.

The memory-safety stakes: agents imitate surrounding patterns, so agentic C++ code can reproduce memory-corruption bugs faster than review — sanitizers (ASan/UBSan) and static analysis are must-have gates.
Agent-readiness is where C++ wins or loses: writing AGENTS.md with deterministic install + discoverable test commands is the single highest-leverage change for agent success.
Tool choice for C++: agentic CLI agents (Claude Code, Aider, Codex) for cross-file refactors vs IDE-composer agents (Cursor, Copilot) for granular edits — plus compiler-aware completions.
C++20/23 features (concepts, ranges, smart pointers, span) give agents guardrails that plain C-style code lacks — modern C++ is more agent-friendly than legacy C.
Practical guardrails: pinned toolchains, sanitizers in CMake, ctest-driven verification loops, and hybrid human-in-the-loop review of every AI-generated pointer/lifetime change.
